title: The plagues (Exodus 7–10)
hookLine: river to blood, frogs, darkness; Pharaoh hardens his heart again and again

cards: Most people know the list, or most of it. The Nile turns to blood, and the fish die. Frogs everywhere: in the bedrooms, the ovens, the kneading bowls.
Then lice. Swarms of flies. A sickness on the livestock.
Boils on people and animals. Hail mixed with fire. Locusts that eat whatever the hail left.
And then darkness so thick it could be felt, for three days. Nine disasters in four chapters. The movies make it a special-effects show.

teach.h: RESPITE, AND HE TAKES IT BACK.
teach.b: Watch Pharaoh. The frogs come, and he begs Moses: take them away, and I'll let the people go. The frogs die.
Then, in the King James Bible: "when Pharaoh saw that there was respite, he hardened his heart, and hearkened not unto them." Relief, and he takes it back. Again and again.
During the hail he even says, I have sinned this time; then the hail stops, and he changes his mind.

teach.h: THIS IS THE FINGER OF GOD.
teach.b: After the lice, his own magicians tell him: "This is the finger of God." He won't hear it.
The Hebrew uses three words for what happens to his heart: it becomes strong, hard, and heavy.
Early on, the text says Pharaoh hardened his own heart, or that his heart was hardened.

Later: "the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh." That has troubled readers for centuries, and Christians answer it differently. Some, drawing on Paul in Romans, stress that God is sovereign even over a king's will.
Others notice that Pharaoh hardens first, many times, and read the later lines as God confirming the choice Pharaoh kept making. Both readings take the text seriously.

And everyone notices the pattern: each no makes the next one easier. Look back over this week: a basket in the reeds, a stranger in Midian, a fire in a bush, I am that I am, five excuses, a request refused.
One man said here am I. Another kept saying no. In the ninth plague, darkness covers Egypt, and the text adds one line: "all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings."

how: Christians often preach on Pharaoh's hardened heart as a warning about repeated refusal, and churches differ on how they explain God hardening it; at the Passover Seder, Jews recite the plagues and spill a drop of wine for each.

games.q: you're Pharaoh. the frogs are gone. you promised to let the people go if they left. now there's relief. what do you do?
games.why: "when Pharaoh saw that there was respite, he hardened his heart." it happens again after nearly every plague.

practice: Think of a person or a subject where your no has become automatic: a relative, an old argument, a part of the news you've stopped feeling anything about.
You don't have to change your mind; just feel the weight there, and ask whether it has grown. If you pray, you can ask for a softer heart; if you don't, simply let the weight be seen.

wordCard.voice: The plagues. The disasters that struck Egypt, from blood in the Nile to three days of darkness, while Pharaoh's heart grew harder each time.

orig.note: Hebrew: heavy. one of the words Exodus uses for Pharaoh's heart; the same root can mean glory.
